title: Why do Brits think 'pants' are underwear? | CLOTHING WORDS

entries.note: The hosts observe that unravel and [[see:ravel]] are contronyms, which makes the show's own title one.
Means much the same as [[see:unravel]], so the pair form a contronym.
A word for underwear, short for [[from:underpants]].
Jess dislikes the word, which was apparently British first; [[from:pantalettes]] were its precursor.
Originally an American term, from [[from:knickerbockers]]; the name passed to [[see:bloomers]] and stuck as the garments got smaller.
Named after [[from:Diedrich Knickerbocker]], the character created by [[see:Washington Irving]], who was illustrated wearing baggy Dutch-style pants gathered at the knee.
[[see:Washington Irving]]'s character, given a deliberately preposterous Dutch-sounding name, who gave his name to [[gave:knickerbockers]].
Writer who brought caricatures of New York's Dutch population to life in satirical fiction, including [[see:Diedrich Knickerbocker]].
A transatlantic rift: American pants shortens [[from:pantaloons]], British pants shortens [[from:underpants]]; both ultimately go back to [[from:Pantalone]].
Literally 'under pantaloons' ([[from:pantaloons]]), and shortened to give British [[gave:pants]] and [[gave:undies]].
A lecherous elderly miser in Italian commedia dell'arte whose bright red skintight leggings gave us [[gave:pantaloons]] and [[gave:pants]].
The French word for trousers, still named after [[from:Pantalone]].
Named after [[from:Pantalone]]; now said mostly humorously, they came between [[see:hose]] and [[see:trousers]] and gave American [[gave:pants]].
Originally a small coat worn under armour, later an underskirt worn under one's 'fashion armour'.
The British word for the sleeveless garment that Americans call a [[equivalent:vest]]; the old sense of coat was close to it.
The American word for what Britons call a [[equivalent:waistcoat]].
A historical undergarment, the precursor to [[gave:panties]].
Underwear so called because you draw them on, which the hosts find rather vague.
A slightly euphemistic word for underwear.
Another slightly euphemistic word for underwear.
A euphemism, discussed in an earlier episode, used for both the private parts and the underwear that covers them.
Voluminous pants worn under a shorter skirt, named after [[from:Amelia Bloomer]] rather than their shape; widely mocked, they lasted only from 1851 to 1855.
A suffragist and women's rights activist who strongly advocated the outfit that became [[gave:bloomers]], and is ironically remembered for pants.
The same word as breeches; related to [[same-root:breach]], to break, maybe for the forked legs or because they were cut off at the knee.
Meaning to break; related to [[same-root:britches]].
A Celtic word from Scotland: a plural of [[from:trews]], already a 'pair', with spelling influenced by French [[see:trousse]]; singular trouser survives in fashion retail.
The original Scottish word behind [[gave:trousers]], related to Irish [[same-root:truis]].
A British cultural reference to [[see:trews]] that always has to be said in a very strong Scottish accent.
The Irish word, spelled out by Rob, alongside Scottish [[same-root:trews]].
Known from French lessons as a pencil case, it could also mean a kind of trouser, and its spelling shaped English [[see:trousers]].
Like other legwear, a 'pair'; short shares its Germanic origin with [[same-root:shirt]] and [[same-root:skirt]].
From Old English, from a Germanic word meaning short; related to [[same-root:shorts]] and [[same-root:skirt]].
Brought by the Vikings from Old Norse, as the sk sound usually was; related to [[same-root:shirt]] and [[same-root:shorts]].
Named after [[from:Genoa]], once called Gene in England; recorded from 1577 in a cargo inventory and first worn as sailors' trousers.
The English name for Italian Genova, once called Gene, spelled G-E-A-N-E, in England; its products gave us [[gave:jeans]].
The one legwear word that isn't plural, though worn in two pieces; it means a tube, the same word as a garden or fireman's hose.
The German word for trousers, used in the plural, unlike singular English [[see:hose]].
Americans still say a pair of pantyhose, showing that [[see:hose]] takes 'a pair of'.
From [[from:serge de Nîmes]]; in Webster's 1864 dictionary it meant a coarse cotton for overalls, as the fabric changed in America but the name stayed.
The original type of serge named after [[from:Nîmes]], which gave [[gave:denim]].
French city near Rob's wife's home, where an airport security guard proudly told travellers their jeans were named after his town ([[gave:serge de Nîmes]]).
A relic of Empire: named after [[from:Dongri]], where Britons bought rugged cotton for sails and tents and later work clothes; Americans say [[equivalent:overalls]].
The usual American word for what the British call [[equivalent:dungarees]].
A hill fort near Bombay where the British traded for tough cotton, giving [[gave:dungarees]].
From the Italian name of [[from:Mosul]], in what is now Iraq.
From the name of [[from:Damascus]] in Syria.
From the Himalayan region of [[from:Kashmir]].
Named after a town in central France where it was first made.
Jess says it was originally a silk from [[from:Tyre]] in Lebanon and went on crusade adventures.
Named after the clan in [[from:Argyll]], Scotland.
Should be [[from:tweel]], the Scots word for twill; English speakers probably confused it with the [[see:River Tweed]].
The Scottish dialect word for twill, misrecorded by the English as [[gave:tweed]].
A river roughly on the England–Scotland border, probably confused with [[see:tweel]] to give [[see:tweed]].
Originally a type of silk, later used for tutus; probably Arabic and possibly named after [[from?:Gaza]], though this is uncertain.
The fabric of the [[from:Seres]], a name for people in northern China who traded silk to the Greeks.
Named after a Chinese place known in Arabic as [[from:Zaitun]].
From Latin [[from:villus]], shaggy hair, ultimately the same origin as [[same-root:velour]].
Ultimately shares its origin with [[same-root:velvet]].
Not New York plus London: [[see:DuPont]]'s Fibre 66 went from [[from:no-run]] to [[from:nuron]], [[from:nulon]] and [[from:nilon]], taking -on from [[see:cotton]] and [[see:rayon]].
Delaware chemicals company that invented and named [[see:nylon]] and still holds the [[see:Lycra]] trademark.
DuPont's working name for the fibre while developing it, before it became [[gave:nylon]].
A rejected name for [[see:nylon]], an acronym of 'DuPont pulls a rabbit out of a hat'; Rob says it sounds like a pooey kangaroo.
With [[see:rayon]], a fibre name ending in -on, which inspired the ending of [[see:nylon]].
With [[see:cotton]], a fibre name ending in -on, which inspired the ending of [[see:nylon]].
One of [[see:DuPont]]'s space-age fibres following the -on pattern of [[see:nylon]].
Another [[see:DuPont]] fibre name with the -on ending of [[see:nylon]].
Another [[see:DuPont]] fibre name with the -on ending of [[see:nylon]].
The DuPont man who proposed [[see:Duparooh]] and then worked through [[see:no-run]], [[see:nuron]], [[see:nulon]] and [[see:nilon]] to reach [[see:nylon]].
Gladding's first idea, meaning the stockings wouldn't [[see:run]], though they did; the first step towards [[gave:nylon]].
The American word for a tear in stockings, which the British call a [[equivalent:ladder]].
The British word for a [[equivalent:run]] in stockings, which Jess thinks makes more sense.
[[from:no-run]] turned around, rejected because it sounded like a nerve tonic.
[[from:nuron]] with L for R, rejected as too close to an existing trademark and because adverts would say 'new nulon'.
[[from:nulon]] with an I, rejected because it had three possible pronunciations, so it was respelled [[gave:nylon]].
A rejected suggestion for [[see:nylon]], which would have named it after Delaware.
From French [[from:gants de Suède]], warm gloves in the Swedish style; the name passed to the material, so wearing suede is wearing 'Swede'.
Gloves of a distinctive cold-resisting material worn in the Swedish style, shortened in England to [[gave:suede]].
Originally meant finely woven, of fabrics and also anything precise; literally a weaving underneath, similar to [[see:underpinning]].
Jess compares it with [[see:subtle]]: something subtle underpins something else.
Being puffed up and dramatic, from [[from:bombast]], cotton padding; possibly covered in an earlier episode.
Originally cotton padding, from Greek [[from:bombyx]], silk or silkworm; gave [[gave:bombastic]].
From weaving: a space rocket evokes the [[from:bobbin]], which has the same shape.
Also a weaving term, like [[see:rocket]]; Rob remembers the shuttle as an important invention from school history.
An anagram of expand because it expands; a proprietary name that has become generic, apparently little used in Europe, where [[equivalent:Lycra]] is more common.
Rob's usual word for [[equivalent:spandex]]; unlike spandex, it is still a registered trademark of [[see:DuPont]].
The generic term for [[equivalent:spandex]], which sounds horrible; its only good anagram Rob found was 'eel Satan'.
From Old French [[from:froc]], a simple coat or monk's habit, later extended to dresses and coats; men originally wore frocks.
Originally menswear, showing that [[see:frock]] once applied to men's garments.
Makes sense given the monk's-habit sense of [[from:frock]]; it doesn't mean simply taking off your frock.
So called because its lined, padded construction is doubled; a tight hip-length jacket going back to the Middle Ages, worn over [[see:hose]] in Tudor times.
Puffy Tudor pants that came before [[see:pantaloons]], worn to show off how much fabric you could afford.
Named after the [[from:7th Earl of Cardigan]], whose men in the Crimean War seem to have pioneered this warm garment.
Led the Charge of the Light Brigade in 1854 and gave his name to the [[gave:cardigan]]; his title comes from [[from:Ceredigion]] in Wales.
Head and face warmer that, like the [[see:cardigan]], comes from Ukraine during the Crimean War.
A place in Wales after which the [[see:7th Earl of Cardigan]]'s title is named, making the [[see:cardigan]] indirectly another garment named after a place.
Clunky rubber rain boots, or wellies, named after [[from:Arthur Wellesley]], Duke of Wellington, though his weren't rubber.
The Duke of Wellington, a British military man after whom the [[gave:Wellington boot]] is named.
The starched, pleated Elizabethan collar, named for its [[from:ruffle]]s; also the fur around an animal's neck.
Jess jokes that, like the [[see:ruff]], it is named for what it does: it busts out your behind.
From French [[from:cravate]], neckwear worn ceremonially by Croatian servicemen; Rob thinks he may have told this story before.
Still the French word for a necktie, from the French word for a [[from:Croat]]; gave English [[gave:cravat]].
From tawdry lace, lace sold at [[from:Saint Audrey]]'s festivals for neckties; it came to mean cheap rustic finery, a word with built-in snobbery.
Lace and ribbons sold around her celebration gave us [[gave:tawdry]].
A very wide hooped Elizabethan skirt; a folk etymology of French [[from:vertugade]], from Spanish [[from:verdugado]], rod or sapling; unrelated to [[unrelated:farthing]] or [[unrelated:gale]].
From French [[from:crin]], horsehair, and [[from:lin]], linen; highly flammable, these skirts are estimated to have burned about 3,000 women alive around the 1840s.
Named after [[from:Bikini Atoll]], an atomic test site; theories include clothes looking blasted off or its explosive effect on men's libidos.
In the Marshall Islands, where the Americans tested the atomic bomb, and the source of the name [[gave:bikini]].
From girls' braids called [[from:flaps]]; once slang for young prostitutes, it became a fashion word from 1895, later used against women wanting the vote, then reclaimed.
Late 1800s word for the braids or ponytails of young girls, unlike women's updos, and the origin of [[gave:flapper]].
Perhaps from [[from?:jack-a-dandy]] or from a pet form of Andrew; a style begun with [[see:Beau Brummell]] that later became an insult, like [[see:macaroni]].
One proposed source for [[gave?:dandy]], which Jess says doesn't really help explain it.
1800s word for women who dressed like male [[see:dandy]] figures; Rob says it sounds like a hybrid flower.
Famously well-dressed Regency figure who started the [[see:dandy]] style of tailored frock coat, white cravat, polished boots and cane.
A recent Met Gala theme: enslaved people dressed opulently by 1700s owners, a style later reclaimed by the [[see:dandy]] movement.
1770s style of towering wigs and tight bright clothes, named after the fancy dish young men brought back from the continent; linked to [[see:Yankee Doodle]].
From [[from:Yankee Doodle]]; originally a foppish, fastidious city man, as in a [[see:dude ranch]], not just any guy.
The ditty in which a feather is called [[see:macaroni]] and Yankee Doodle is a [[see:dandy]]; it gave us [[gave:dude]].
A holiday ranch where city types, the original [[see:dude]]s, could experience the Old West.
Fashionable young aristocratic men after the Terror, in big cravats and tight breeches; partners to the [[see:Merveilleuses]].
Fashionable aristocratic women after the Terror who wore sheer white and pastel muslin; counterparts of the [[see:Incroyables]].
